name: Task Queue (Celery-Style)
description: Design a distributed task queue system like Celery. Covers async job submission, priority queuing, worker pools, retries with backoff, result storage, and dead-letter handling.

learnSteps.title: Asynchronous Task Submission
learnSteps.description: The Application Server receives a request (e.g., generate a report, process an image) and immediately publishes a task message to RabbitMQ with a unique task ID, payload, priority, and retry policy. It returns HTTP 202 Accepted with the task ID so the client can poll for results. This decouples the request lifecycle from the task execution, keeping API response times under 50ms regardless of task complexity.

learnSteps.title: Priority Queues and Routing
learnSteps.description: RabbitMQ maintains multiple queues with different priorities (critical, high, normal, low). Tasks are routed to queues via exchange bindings based on task type and priority header. Workers consume from higher-priority queues first using consumer priority settings. This ensures time-sensitive tasks (password resets, payment confirmations) are processed ahead of bulk jobs (report generation, data exports).

learnSteps.title: Worker Pool Execution and Concurrency
learnSteps.description: 20 worker instances each run 8 concurrent greenlet/threads, giving 160 parallel task slots. Workers prefetch a small batch (4 messages) to minimize idle time. Each task runs inside a timeout wrapper -- if a task exceeds 5 minutes it is killed and re-queued. Workers report heartbeats; if a worker dies mid-task, RabbitMQ redelivers the unacknowledged message to another worker. Results and artifacts are written to PostgreSQL and S3 respectively.

learnSteps.title: Retries, Dead Letters, and Observability
learnSteps.description: Failed tasks are retried with exponential backoff (1s, 4s, 16s) up to 3 attempts. After max retries, tasks move to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for manual inspection. Each task state transition (pending, started, retry, success, failure) is logged to PostgreSQL with timestamps, enabling dashboards to show queue depth, throughput, p99 latency, and failure rates. Alerting fires when the DLQ grows or queue depth exceeds thresholds.

chaosScenarios.name: RabbitMQ Memory Watermark Breach
chaosScenarios.description: Queue backlog grows until the broker hits its memory high watermark and blocks all publishers, freezing the API submit path
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Publisher connections are blocked, so Application Server publish calls hang until timeout. Task submission latency jumps from 25ms to the full 30s gateway timeout. Consumers keep draining, so the alarm clears once depth drops below the watermark.
mitigationSteps: Page immediately — blocked publishers means the synchronous API path is down
Convert hot queues to lazy mode so backlog pages to disk instead of RAM
Scale the worker pool to accelerate drain
Apply queue length limits with overflow=reject-publish so future overload fails fast instead of blocking

chaosScenarios.name: Worker Pool Mass Failure
chaosScenarios.description: A bad deploy OOM-kills half the worker fleet mid-task; unacknowledged messages must be redelivered to survivors
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: RabbitMQ detects dropped connections and redelivers ~80 in-flight unacked messages to surviving workers. Queue depth climbs as 50% of drain capacity disappears. Non-idempotent tasks that had side effects before dying execute twice.
mitigationSteps: Roll back the deploy and let autoscaling replace dead instances
Verify redelivered messages carry the redelivered flag so idempotency guards engage
Audit tasks with external side effects (emails, payments) for duplicates
Hold queue-depth alerts in acknowledged state until drain rate normalizes

chaosScenarios.name: Poison Message Redelivery Loop
chaosScenarios.description: A malformed payload crashes the consuming worker process before it can ack or reject, so the broker redelivers it to the next worker, serially crashing the fleet
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: One message cycles through workers causing repeated crashes; throughput on the affected queue drops as workers spend time restarting. Retry counter in the message header eventually routes it to the DLQ after 3 attempts — if the crash happens before retry accounting, the loop is unbounded.
mitigationSteps: Identify the message via worker crash logs and correlation IDs
Use x-death headers / delivery-count quarantine so broker-side limits apply even when workers crash pre-ack
Move the message to the DLQ manually and restore the queue
Patch payload validation to reject the malformed shape at publish time

bottleneckProgression.description: 160 concurrent task slots saturate; queue depth begins growing faster than drain rate
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale worker instances on queue depth, not CPU — queue depth leads CPU as the demand signal

bottleneckProgression.description: Backlogged classic queues hold messages in broker RAM, approaching the memory watermark
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Enable lazy queues, set per-queue length limits, and shard hot queues across the cluster

bottleneckProgression.description: Result writes from a scaled-out worker fleet exhaust PostgreSQL's 200-connection limit
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Front the result store with PgBouncer in transaction mode and batch state-transition writes

expectedIssues.title: Unbounded Queue Growth
expectedIssues.description: Producers are decoupled from consumers, so nothing inherently stops submission when workers fall behind — backlog grows until broker memory or disk is exhausted
expectedIssues.mitigation: Queue length limits with reject-publish overflow, publisher confirms, and autoscaling keyed to queue depth

expectedIssues.title: Duplicate Task Execution
expectedIssues.description: At-least-once delivery means a worker that dies after performing side effects but before acking causes the task to run again on another worker
expectedIssues.mitigation: Idempotency keys checked against the result store before side effects; design all tasks to be safely re-runnable

expectedIssues.title: Low-Priority Starvation and Head-of-Line Blocking
expectedIssues.description: Sustained critical-priority traffic starves bulk queues indefinitely, and long-running tasks occupy prefetched slots that block queued short tasks behind them
expectedIssues.mitigation: Dedicated worker pools per task class (short vs long-running) and minimum drain quotas for low-priority queues

expectedIssues.title: Result Store Bloat
expectedIssues.description: Every task writes state transitions and results to PostgreSQL; at 5k tasks/s the table grows by hundreds of millions of rows per week, degrading status-poll queries
expectedIssues.mitigation: Time-partitioned task tables with a TTL drop policy; move large results to S3 and store only pointers

steps: Compare drain rate vs publish rate to confirm it is a capacity problem, not a stuck consumer
Check worker fleet health — crashed consumers look identical to slow ones in depth graphs
Identify the dominant slow task type via task_duration by type
Scale workers; if broker memory is at risk, enable lazy queues before adding publishers
Shed or defer low-priority publishes until depth recovers
Confirm publisher connections are in blocked state — API latency will show it first
Enable lazy mode on the deepest queues to page backlog to disk
Scale workers to maximum to accelerate drain
After recovery, set queue length limits so overload rejects instead of blocking
Correlate worker crash timestamps with a single message ID
Pull the message into the DLQ and confirm worker crash loop stops
Reproduce the deserialization failure locally from the DLQ payload
Ship a publish-side validation fix and replay or discard the message

decisions.title: Asynchronous 202-Accepted Submission
decisions.context: Task execution time varies from milliseconds to minutes; holding HTTP connections open for task completion would exhaust server connections
decisions.decision: Publish to the broker and return 202 with a task ID immediately; clients poll the result store for completion
consequences: API latency stays under 50ms regardless of task complexity
Clients must implement polling or webhooks
A result store becomes mandatory infrastructure

decisions.title: At-Least-Once Delivery with Idempotent Tasks
decisions.context: Exactly-once execution across a distributed broker and worker fleet is not achievable without distributed transactions
decisions.decision: Accept redelivery of unacked messages and require all tasks to be idempotent
consequences: No task is silently lost when workers die
Tasks with external side effects need explicit idempotency keys
Duplicate-execution auditing becomes part of incident response

decisions.title: Priority Queues with Per-Class Worker Routing
decisions.context: Password resets and payment confirmations cannot wait behind hour-long report generation jobs
decisions.decision: Route tasks to priority-tiered queues via exchange bindings, with consumer priorities favoring critical queues
consequences: Time-sensitive tasks start within seconds even under bulk load
Sustained critical traffic can starve bulk queues without drain quotas
Queue topology becomes configuration that must be kept in sync with task definitions

tradeoffs.benefit: No lost tasks, no distributed transaction machinery
tradeoffs.cost: Every task author carries the idempotency burden; duplicates surface as user-visible bugs when they forget

tradeoffs.choice: PostgreSQL result backend instead of broker-native or Redis results
tradeoffs.benefit: Rich status queries, dashboards, and audit history with SQL
tradeoffs.cost: Every task adds DB writes; the result store becomes a scaling bottleneck before the broker does

tradeoffs.benefit: Workers rarely idle waiting on broker round-trips
tradeoffs.cost: Prefetched messages are invisible to other workers, so a slow task delays its prefetched neighbors

alternatives.name: Redis as Broker
alternatives.description: Use Redis lists or streams as the task transport instead of RabbitMQ
alternatives.prosVsCons: Operationally lighter and very fast, but weaker delivery semantics — no per-message acks with broker-side redelivery accounting, and failover can drop in-flight messages
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Reliability requirements (redelivery on worker death, DLQ routing, publisher confirms) map directly to RabbitMQ features

alternatives.name: Kafka as Broker
alternatives.description: Publish tasks to Kafka topics consumed by worker groups
alternatives.prosVsCons: Higher throughput and replayable history, but no per-message ack — one slow task blocks its partition, and consumer-group rebalances pause the whole fleet
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Heterogeneous task durations make head-of-line blocking per partition unacceptable; queue semantics fit better than log semantics

alternatives.name: Serverless Functions (Lambda-style)
alternatives.description: Execute each task as a function invocation triggered from the queue
alternatives.prosVsCons: Zero fleet management and instant scale-out, but 15-minute execution caps, cold starts, and per-invocation pricing that exceeds reserved workers at this sustained volume
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Long-running tasks (5-minute timeout today, batch jobs tomorrow) and steady 5k RPS volume favor a reserved worker fleet
